newsitem.title: USA: Donations to the Clintons' legal fund dwindling.
newsitem.headline: Donations to the Clintons' legal fund dwindling.

text.p: Donations to the legal defence fund for President Bill Clinton and Hillary Rodham Clinton have dwindled, with more than $2.25 million in lawyer bills unpaid at the end of 1996, a fund trustee said on Thursday.

The fund, known as the Presidental Legal Expense Trust, took in $62,045 in donations between July and December of last year, "by far the lowest amount in any six-month period" since it was started in June 1994, trustee Michael Cardozo said.

At the White House, spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton was "painfully aware of those facts." McCurry indicated Clinton "expects to honour his obligation to pay those bills" after he leaves the presidency.

Acknowledging that the fund's own strict rules -- solicitation of funds is forbidden and individual donations cannot exceed $1,000 -- have kept the coffers bare, Cardozo told reporters establishment of a second fund with different, potentially lighter restrictions was a possibility.
"The White House counsel's office is aware of that option," he told a news conference.

Another setback was the trust's rejection last year of some $640,000 in contributions brought in by Charles Yah Lin Trie, he said. Trie, a Little Rock, Arkansas, restauranteur and longtime Clinton friend, funnelled the funds through some contributors who, in Cardozo's words, had an "inherent implausibility" to give such large sums of money.
A sheriff's office clerk and a manicurist were among donors linked to Trie who contributed $500 or $1,000, and that made the trustees uncomfortable enough to reject all such donations, Cardozo said.

Trie also helped get a visa for a Chinese arms merchant whose company was implicated in a gun smuggling scheme so he could attend a White House reception a year ago. Clinton later denounced the visit as inappropriate.
Some of those whose funds were rejected were unaffiliated with Trie. Some were ineligible because they were government employees, who are not permitted to contribute under the terms of the trust.
References to these rejected donors were left out of the mountain of campaign financing documents released by the White House this week to spare the donors embarrassment, the trustees said.

The trust released a complete list of donors whose funds were accepted in the last half of 1996 and Cardozo said he recognised "three or four names" from this list that were also on the list of overnight White House guests released on Tuesday, but he said this was not significant.

The defence fund was set up to defray costs of defending the Clintons on any charges related to the Whitewater land deal affair dating back to their Arkansas days as well as the sexual harassment case brought against the president by Paula Jones.
It was later determined that legal costs of the Jones matter would be paid by the Clintons' liability insurance.

More than $3 million in legal expenses have been turned over to the defence trust but only $766,134 has been paid, leaving a balance of $2.25 million. The Clintons' lawyers are some of the most prestigious and expensive in the country, and Cardozo said this was justified.
"It's the two of them against this incredible army of lawyers, accountants and the media, scrutinising it, and they need the best help they can get," he said.
